question: Can the onset and early growth of romantic feelings be modeled as a mean-field second-order phase transition, with love at first sight following a square-root order-parameter law and pre-existing liking acting as an external bias?

key_findings.claim: The paper maps romantic feeling intensity to the order parameter of a quartic Landau potential and assumes that its quadratic coefficient decreases linearly with time.
key_findings.evidence: With F(alpha)=F0+h alpha+A alpha squared+B alpha to the fourth, zero bias, positive B, and A proportional to negative elapsed time, minimizing F yields alpha proportional to the square root of time after threshold. A nonzero h removes the exact zero-feeling phase and rounds the transition, which the authors interpret as love developing from liking or friendship.

anchors.section: IV Love from Liking, Equation 4 and Figure 3

key_findings.claim: Ratings of hand-picked literary phrases can be made visually consistent with square-root growth, but the design does not identify a universal exponent for real romantic love.
key_findings.evidence: Six to ten raters aged 40-83 score selected consecutive passages from three works on a 0-10 scale. The authors normalize each work's maximum to one, assume equal time between phrases, fit an unreported transition moment per book, and then pool the normalized points to estimate an exponent 0.56 plus or minus 0.06. Phrase selection, equal spacing, transition placement, and maximum normalization are all researcher-controlled, and the observations are fictional depictions rather than repeated measurements of people falling in love.

anchors.section: III Love at First Sight, literary-rating protocol and Figure 2

key_findings.claim: The Jane Eyre and private-diary fits illustrate the biased model, but neither constitutes an independent prospective test.
key_findings.evidence: For Jane Eyre, the authors date selected paragraphs, choose day 28 as the transition because a strong change is visible, set the final selected day as the time scale, normalize the maximum, and fit h near -0.68. For the diary, one respondent retrospectively scores one 137-day episode without independent raters; the transition is defined as the day the normalized score reaches 0.5 and h is then fit near -0.15. Reported p-values do not remove this post-selection or establish comparison against flexible monotone alternatives.

anchors.section: Appendix B Jane Eyre selected passages

key_findings.claim: The data do not measure a neural critical point, dopamine, serotonin, excitation-inhibition balance, susceptibility, or any other physical state variable needed to establish the proposed brain mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: The empirical variables are third-party ratings of prose and one retrospective diary rating series. The link from love to increased dopamine, reduced serotonin, and a switch from critical to supercritical brain dynamics is proposed from prior literature, while the paper itself collects no neural, hormonal, pharmacological, behavioral-intervention, or physiological measurement.

anchors.section: III Love at First Sight, neurochemical hypothesis
Discussion, need for direct brain measurements

key_findings.claim: The square-root curve follows from untested mean-field equilibrium assumptions rather than uniquely from the second-order-transition hypothesis.
key_findings.evidence: The exponent one-half requires a symmetric quartic potential, positive constant B, h=0, a coefficient A linear in time, and quasi-static equilibration. The paper acknowledges divergent relaxation and the Kibble-Zurek mechanism but sets them aside, and it does not compare other critical exponents, non-equilibrium dynamics, smooth growth curves, change-point models, or stochastic relationship models. Many monotone saturating trajectories could fit the sparse normalized ratings.

anchors.section: Mean-field scaling and quasi-static time assumption

key_findings.claim: The proposed threshold between love-hate bistability and stable friendship-based love is an anecdotal model interpretation, not a validated relationship forecast.
key_findings.evidence: The cubic discriminant yields a critical absolute bias around 0.44 after a chosen normalization. The fitted Jane Eyre bias exceeds it and the diary bias falls below it; the authors then match those classifications to the novel's ending and a relationship that ended after one year. Both outcomes were available during model construction, there are only two examples, and h has no external measurement independent of the same feeling trajectory.

method.core_idea: Reuse a scalar Landau free-energy expansion as a phenomenological cost function for romantic feelings, derive its equilibrium order parameter during a linear time quench, and compare the resulting curves with normalized ratings of literary and diary passages.
method.mechanism: At zero external bias, the quartic potential changes from one minimum at zero to two symmetry-broken minima when A changes sign, producing square-root growth. A nonzero bias h tilts the potential, gives a nonzero pre-threshold feeling, rounds the transition, and changes whether one or three stationary roots exist. Literary raters supply feeling scores and fitted transition times or h values align examples to those curves.
assumptions: Romantic feeling intensity is a one-dimensional order parameter with a meaningful negative branch interpreted as hate.
A person's relevant neural state is close enough to equilibrium that minimizing a static Landau potential at each time is appropriate.
The quadratic coefficient crosses zero linearly in elapsed time and higher-order or asymmetric terms can be neglected.
Sequential phrases chosen from novels accurately sample real within-person feeling trajectories at equal time intervals.
Ratings from small convenience groups share a common cardinal scale after within-story maximum normalization.
The fitted external bias is an identifiable property of pre-existing liking rather than a generic curve-shape parameter.

techniques.role: Transfers a quartic symmetry-breaking potential from statistical physics into a scalar phenomenological model of affect.
Assumes the control coefficient varies linearly with time to derive mean-field square-root growth after the transition.
Turns selected prose descriptions into small-panel numerical estimates of a character's feeling intensity.
Uses the stationary cubic and its discriminant to distinguish rounded growth from a three-root love/indifference/hate interpretation.

evaluations.setting: Selected consecutive passages from Romeo and Juliet, The Lily of the Valley, and Martin Eden rated by six to ten respondents per text.
evaluations.metric: Normalized feeling intensity versus assumed equally spaced narrative time; pooled log-log exponent.
evaluations.result: The plotted points are visually compatible with square-root growth and the pooled fitted exponent is reported as 0.56 plus or minus 0.06.
evaluations.baseline: The mean-field zero-bias prediction alpha proportional to the square root of time; no alternative growth family is fitted.

evaluations.setting: Selected, approximately dated Jane Eyre paragraphs spanning 45 days.
evaluations.metric: Fit of the nonzero-bias Landau solution to normalized ratings.
evaluations.result: The paper reports h approximately -0.68 plus or minus 0.08 and p=4e-5 after choosing day 28 as transition and day 45 as the normalized endpoint.
evaluations.baseline: The rounded-transition curve with one fitted bias; no holdout passages or competing nonlinear model.

evaluations.setting: One person's retrospective scoring of one 137-day relationship episode recorded in a private 1970s diary.
evaluations.metric: Fit of normalized scores to the biased-transition curve.
evaluations.result: The paper reports h approximately -0.15 plus or minus 0.05 and p=4e-3, without inter-rater error bars and after defining the transition from the same series.
evaluations.baseline: The biased Landau curve; no independent rating, prospective forecast, or alternative trajectory model.

evaluations.setting: Post hoc comparison of fitted h with a normalized critical magnitude near 0.44.
evaluations.metric: Whether the example relationship is placed in the model's one-root or three-root regime.
evaluations.result: Jane Eyre is classified as strongly biased and durable, while the diary case is classified as capable of ending; both are matched to already-known narrative outcomes.
evaluations.baseline: The cubic discriminant threshold, not an externally validated predictor.

limitations: Author-stated: the small number of books is not definitive, reading and translation change phrase perception, the diary has no multi-rater uncertainty, and direct brain-activity studies are still required.
Reviewer inference: the study has no human participants observed while falling in love and therefore cannot test a neural phase transition.
Reviewer inference: phrase selection, time assignment, transition placement, normalization, and outcome interpretation create enough analytic flexibility to favor the proposed curve.
Reviewer inference: p-values are reported without a clear null, likelihood, residual model, multiple-comparison treatment, or out-of-sample prediction target.
Reviewer inference: the mean-field exponent is not robust to non-equilibrium critical slowing, dimensionality, finite-size effects, asymmetric potentials, or alternative affect dynamics.
Reviewer inference: love, liking, hate, arousal, attachment, relationship satisfaction, and partner preference are treated as positions on one scale despite being distinct constructs.
failure_modes: A monotone but noncritical feeling trajectory can appear square-root-like after choosing a transition origin and rescaling its maximum.
Selected literary language can intensify for narrative reasons even if the represented character state does not follow the same time course.
Small rater panels can share cultural expectations about how famous romances develop, making ratings non-independent of the hypothesis's familiar shape.
A fitted bias may absorb arbitrary early offset, saturation, or timing error and then appear to predict stability through a threshold derived from that same parameterization.
Neural criticality at one spatial or temporal scale would not imply that a high-level psychological construct is its order parameter.
Dopamine and serotonin can change during reward, attachment, arousal, and stress without generating the specific symmetry-breaking transition asserted here.
reusable_insights: A physical analogy becomes testable only after its control parameter, order parameter, perturbation response, and critical exponents are operationalized independently.
Narrative or diary data can generate hypotheses about temporal affect, but prospective intensive longitudinal measurement is needed before mechanistic interpretation.
Criticality claims should test several linked signatures—scaling, susceptibility, slowing, correlation length, and perturbation response—not fit one power-law exponent.
Model comparison must include flexible noncritical trajectories and freeze preprocessing decisions before outcome data are examined.
open_questions: Do prospectively sampled feelings, physiology, hormones, and neural activity around relationship onset exhibit a common preregistered change point and linked critical exponents?
Can the proposed external bias be measured before onset from independently assessed familiarity, attraction, or friendship strength and predict a held-out trajectory?
Does a square-root law outperform splines, logistic growth, Bayesian change points, stochastic differential equations, and reinforcement-learning value updates on new couples?
What perturbation would measure a diverging susceptibility near romantic onset without unethical manipulation or retrospective inference?
Are love, attachment, desire, idealization, and hate better represented by a multivariate state space than by a signed scalar order parameter?
Would the fitted results survive blinded phrase sampling, independent time coding, larger diverse rater panels, and preregistered normalization?

competitive_landscape.title: Stochastic Nonlinear Dynamics of Interpersonal and Romantic Relationships
competitive_landscape.difference: Cherif and Barley model interpersonal dynamics with deterministic and stochastic differential equations that permit oscillations and transitions between stable equilibria; the phase-transition paper instead imposes a scalar equilibrium Landau potential and one mean-field growth exponent, with much less treatment of noise and reciprocal partners.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamic corticostriatal activity biases social bonding in monogamous female prairie voles
competitive_landscape.difference: Amadei et al. measure mPFC-to-nucleus-accumbens dynamics during bond formation and causally bias later partner preference with circuit stimulation in prairie voles; the phase-transition paper has human-romance relevance but no neural measurement or intervention and cannot localize its proposed order parameter.

competitive_landscape.title: Investigating real-life emotions in romantic couples: a mobile EEG study
competitive_landscape.difference: This mobile-EEG study measures partners during real-life emotional interaction, providing synchronized neural and experiential observations; the Landau study substitutes ratings of fictional prose and one private diary for direct couple-level physiology and thus cannot test neural criticality.

competitive_landscape.title: Theoretical foundations of studying criticality in the brain
competitive_landscape.difference: Tian et al. distinguish ordinary, quasi-, self-organized, and self-organized quasi-criticality and catalogue validity failures in inferring them from neural data; those criteria make clear that a single fitted affect exponent without avalanches, control parameters, or neural observables is insufficient evidence for brain criticality.

competitive_landscape.title: Mating proximity blinds threat perception
competitive_landscape.difference: This work experimentally traces how courtship proximity biases threat processing in an animal neural circuit, offering a causal route to the 'love blindness' phenomenon; the phase-transition paper explains the proverb through supercritical insensitivity without measuring perception, circuit state, or a transition.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that romantic love may be a naturally occurring second-order transition in the brain and that one Landau model unifies love at first sight, love from friendship, love-hate switching, and relationship durability.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Sparse normalized ratings from three novels, one additional novel, and one diary can be aligned with zero- and nonzero-bias equilibrium curves.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The novel element is the explicit Landau mapping and its memorable qualitative predictions. It should be treated as a speculative hypothesis generator, not evidence of a neural phase transition: direct neuroscience, stochastic relationship models, and modern criticality methodology provide stronger measurement and falsification standards.

reviewer_notes: I reviewed all eight extracted pages, equations, rating procedures, figures, appendices, and cited interpretive claims. The mathematical derivations are read as conditional consequences of the chosen potential; my contradiction audits address empirical identification and post hoc degrees of freedom, not algebra alone. Competing and adjacent records were checked on official arXiv or Nature pages on 2026-08-23.
